title: What Photo 51 Could Say
paragraphs: The most famous image in molecular biology is a dark field crossed by a blurred X of dashes; to an untrained eye, Photo 51 could pass for a flaw in the film.
It was recorded at King's College London in May 1952, and within a year it had helped settle the shape of DNA.
The story is usually told as the triumph of James Watson and Francis Crick in Cambridge, and their model deserves its fame.
But the model rested on measurements made by other people, and how they traveled between laboratories has been argued over ever since.
Friedrich Miescher isolated DNA from the nuclei of white blood cells in 1869, but for decades nobody took it seriously.
The biochemist Phoebus Levene later identified its parts: a sugar, a phosphate group, and the four bases adenine, guanine, cytosine, and thymine.
Levene proposed that the four bases simply repeated in a fixed order along the chain, the tetranucleotide hypothesis, and a molecule that monotonous seemed too dull to carry hereditary instructions.
Proteins, built from some twenty different amino acids, looked a far better candidate.
The mood changed in 1944, when Oswald Avery and his colleagues showed that purified DNA could pass a heritable trait between strains of bacteria.
The tetranucleotide hypothesis fell to careful chemistry.
In the late 1940s Erwin Chargaff at Columbia University used paper chromatography to separate and measure the four bases in the DNA of many species.
First, the proportions of the bases differed from one species to another, which a fixed repeating unit could not allow.
Second, in every sample the amount of adenine closely matched the amount of thymine, and guanine matched cytosine.
These became known as Chargaff's ratios; he reported them without explaining them.
Shape was a question for X-rays: when a beam passes through a fiber of roughly parallel long molecules, the regularly spaced atoms scatter it into a pattern of spots and arcs on film.
The pattern is not an image of the molecule; it is a map of the distances that repeat inside it, and turning it back into a structure takes mathematics and judgment.

In 1938 William Astbury and Florence Bell at Leeds recorded the first X-ray patterns from DNA fibers and found a strong repeat of 3.4 angstroms along the fiber axis, but their fibers were too poorly ordered to say more.
The problem passed to King's College London, where the physicist John Randall ran a biophysics unit.
His deputy, Maurice Wilkins, and a graduate student, Raymond Gosling, had already obtained sharper DNA patterns than Astbury's.
In January 1951 Rosalind Franklin joined the unit.
Trained as a physical chemist at Cambridge, she had spent three years in Paris learning to apply X-ray methods, and Randall assigned her the DNA problem, with Gosling as her student.
Wilkins seems to have expected her to work as his assistant; she understood from Randall's letter that the problem was now hers.
The misunderstanding was never repaired.

Franklin found that DNA fibers take two forms: at lower humidity the molecule packs into an ordered, crystalline arrangement she called the A form, and with more water it loosens into the less ordered B form of living cells.
Controlling the moisture, she and Gosling photographed each form alone, and in May 1952 Gosling, under her direction, recorded the B form image that became Photo 51.
To anyone trained in the new diffraction theory of helices, the picture was eloquent.

The X of dashes meant a helix; the spacing between the dashes gave the distance the helix climbs in one full turn, 34 angstroms; the heavy smudges at top and bottom gave the 3.4 angstrom spacing between stacked bases; and the width of the pattern gave the molecule's diameter, about 20 angstroms.
Franklin did not rush to build a model.
The B form was plainly helical, but the A form promised more exact numbers, and she set out to extract them by Patterson analysis, a slow method that assumes nothing in advance.
She distrusted guesswork, and in July 1952 she and Gosling circulated a mock death notice for the crystalline DNA helix, a joke often read, unfairly, as denying that DNA was helical at all.
What she lacked was not insight but a reason to hurry.
Watson and Crick, at Cambridge's Cavendish Laboratory, worked in the opposite spirit.
Following the example of Linus Pauling, who had found the alpha helix of proteins in 1951 by building models, they guessed the structure first and tested it against the X-ray data afterward.
Their first attempt, in November 1951, was a three-chain helix with the phosphates on the inside.
Franklin, visiting from London, pointed out that it allowed for only a fraction of the water her measurements showed the fibers to contain, and the model was abandoned.
Lawrence Bragg, the laboratory's director, ordered the pair to leave DNA to King's.
They were let back in early in 1953, after Pauling produced a three-chain model with the same flaw and seemed likely to correct it.
Three pieces of evidence then reached Watson and Crick.
In January 1953 Wilkins showed Watson Photo 51 without telling Franklin, and Watson, who knew the helical theory, read the X at a glance.

In February Max Perutz of the Cavendish passed Crick a committee report with Franklin's measurements, among them the symmetry of the A form crystals, from which Crick deduced that the two chains ran in opposite directions.
Finally Jerry Donohue, a chemist sharing their office, corrected the textbook forms of the bases Watson had been using.
With the right forms, Watson found in late February that an adenine-thymine pair and a guanine-cytosine pair were the same width, so any sequence fit between two evenly spaced backbones.
Chargaff's ratios fell out of the geometry at once: if adenine always faces thymine, the two must be equally abundant.
The result appeared in Nature on April 25, 1953, in about nine hundred words, alongside papers from Wilkins's group and from Franklin and Gosling.

Watson and Crick described two chains wound around a common axis, backbones outside and paired bases inside, joined by hydrogen bonds between the bases, and added a sentence quoted ever since: the specific pairing immediately suggested a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.
They acknowledged being stimulated by a general knowledge of unpublished results from King's; they did not say how much they had seen.
Franklin had left for Birkbeck College in London, where she turned to the structure of viruses.
She died of ovarian cancer in April 1958, at the age of thirty-seven.

In 1962 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins; a prize is shared by at most three people and is not given to anyone who died before being nominated, so the question of whether she would have been included was never put.
The argument over credit began in 1968 with Watson's memoir The Double Helix, which treated Franklin as an obstacle.
Anne Sayre's biography of 1975 answered it, and a story took shape in which Franklin's photograph was stolen and her discovery taken from her.
That story is too simple, and I think it does her a disservice.
Her Birkbeck colleague Aaron Klug, reading her notebooks, showed that she had worked out several features of the double helix herself and was, in his judgment, close to the full structure.
She was less a victim of theft than a contributor whose share was quietly forgotten, a harder wrong to put right.
What strikes me most is how little a single image could settle.
Photo 51 said helix and gave three numbers; it did not say how many chains there were, which way they ran, or how the bases fit together.

Those answers came from the symmetry in Franklin's crystallographic report, from Chargaff's ratios, from Donohue's chemistry, and from two impatient men who kept building wrong models until one was right.
The double helix was the meeting point of two methods, the patient measurement that Franklin practiced and the bold guessing that she distrusted, and neither would have finished the job alone.
That is a less satisfying story than a theft or a triumph, but I suspect it is the true one.
